newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerians vote in test military's democracy plan.
newsitem.headline: Nigerians vote in test military's democracy plan.

text.p: More than 55 million voters head for the polls in Nigeria on Saturday in local elections held out by the ruling generals as proof of their commitment to return the populous nation to democracy.
An official statement said security forces were on maximum alert and would, if need be, "deal ruthlessly with any cases of malpractice or misconduct at polling centres".
The poll to elect chairmen and councillors in more than 770 town halls is the first multi-party ballot since General Sani Abacha seized power in November 1993.
The last vote to end the Nigerian army's long stranglehold on power ended in fiasco. The military abruptly scrapped the June 1993 presidential poll as a winner emerged.
Abacha seized power in the confusion that ensued, and Nigeria plunged further into crisis after he jailed the presumed winner of the election, southern businessman Moshood Abiola.

Abacha stamped out the unrest that swept Abiola's southwestern power base but his own plan to return Nigeria to democracy in 1998 has been denounced by pro-democracy activists and viewed with scepticism in the West.
No established international or Western monitoring groups have been invited to observe the elections although a 30-member U.S. team of mostly African Americans arrived this week.
The government has been shunned by Western powers since the 1995 hanging of writer Ken Saro Wiwa and eight other minority activists after a special court convicted them of murder.
But judging by the massive registration for the vote, the enthusiasm of Nigerians for elections has not diminished.
The National Electoral Commission of Nigeria (NECON) released final figures showing nearly 56 million voters had been registered for the poll from a population of about 100 million.
"NECON has made all necessary arrangements to ensure a successful poll," the commission's public affairs director Steve Osemeke said in a statement on Friday.
Candidates from the country's five registered parties campaigned feverishly up to midnight on Thursday.
Pro-democracy groups who denounce the military's democracy programme as a sham urged people to ignore local elections held exactly a year ago on non-party basis as a test run.
This time they have not urged a boycott but neither have they shown any enthusiasm for the ballot.
Political analysts say many opponents and critics of the government may not vote because their parties were not registered.
But they, like many other Nigerians, will be waiting to see the trend that emerges from the local elections to decide their political affiliation for other elections on the transition timetable.

Under Abacha's democracy programme, elections at state level will be held in the third quarter of the year. National elections are scheduled for next year, culminating in a presidential poll and the handover of power to an elected civilian president on October 1, 1998.

Political instability and military intervention have dogged Nigeria since independence from Britain in 1960, partly explaining its inability to harness its vast oil wealth. The army has held power for most of the time since 1960.
Speculation is rife that Abacha will contest next year's presidential election to turn himself into an elected leader.
Polls open at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) and close at 4 p.m. (1500 GMT). Early returns are expected from Sunday but definitive results may take some days.
